original.source: This manuscript constructs the one-loop quantum Batalin–Vilkovisky theory of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills theory on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, together with the transformations of its local operators under the whole superconformal algebra, in the renormalisation formalism of Costello [C07] and Costello–Gwilliam [CG2]. The single regulator is a lower cutoff $\varepsilon>0$ on Schwinger time, the ultraviolet (UV) boundary; the upper end of every Schwinger integral is $\infty$, so that $\varepsilon$ is the single scale of the construction. This overview states what is constructed, where the construction needs care, how the chapters are organised, and the results of this first step.

The fields are those of ten-dimensional super Yang–Mills theory reduced to $\mathbb R^4$ [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], complexified. Write $V$ for the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$ and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ for the six transverse directions, and $\mathfrak g$ for the complexified gauge Lie algebra with its invariant pairing $(-,-)$, which carries the coupling. The gauge field $A$ is a ten-component one-form with values in $\mathfrak g$: its components along $V$ form the connection $A|_V$, and its components $\iota_wA$, $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, are the six scalars. The gaugino $\lambda$ takes values in the ten-dimensional semi-spin representation $\Sigma$, which in four dimensions is $S_+\otimes W\oplus S_-\otimes W^*$, with $S_\pm$ the two Weyl spinor representations and $W$ the four-dimensional R-symmetry space [ESW, §10]; spinors stay index free throughout. The ghost $c$ and the antifields $A^*$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$ complete the fields [ESW, Def 3.2, Rem 1.36]. The action $S$ is [ESW, (31)] reduced to four dimensions; its quadratic part defines the linear differential $Q$, the rest is the interaction $I$, and $\{-,-\}$ is the odd Poisson bracket [C07, Lemma 4.3.2].

Costello's construction needs three more objects. A gauge-fixing operator $Q^{GF}$ [C07, §1.1, Def 4.3.3], here of Feynman type, makes $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$ [C07, Def 4.3.3(4)] the Laplacian on every field. The heat kernel $K_t$ of $H$ at Schwinger time $t$ [C07, §6.5] gives the propagator

with $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ the second-order operator contracting two fields with the kernel $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ [C07, §6.4]; this is the functional called $\Gamma$ in [C07, Def 6.6.1]. As in Theorem B of [C07], whose analogue on $\mathbb R^4$ with upper scale $\infty$ Chapter 4 proves at one loop, the counterterm $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is the singular part of the graph expansion, extracted graph by graph, with coefficients in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ at one loop; it is local by power counting in the Schwinger times, it is unique, and $W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\big)$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$. A local operator $O$, for instance $\int\omega\,(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$ with $\omega$ a compactly supported four-form [CG2, Lemma 10.1.1.3], enters through a square-zero parameter $\delta$ [CG2, Def 8.3.1.1]: the counterterm $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ of the family $I+\delta O$ defines the local operator at the UV end, $O(\varepsilon)=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, and its quantum observable is

The superconformal algebra $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ [SW, (7), (17)] acts through an equivariant action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, a Maurer–Cartan element of the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of [ESW, Def 1.26–1.27] with differential $d_{CE}$. Building $O[\infty]$ from the equivariant interaction, the transformation of $O$ along a generator $x_1\in\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is the component $[(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]](x_1)$. Along the dilatation $\Delta$, the generator $2E$ of [SW, (17)] with $E$ the Euler vector field [SW, (3)], it is the anomalous dimension; along the supercharges $Q^i_\alpha$, $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha i}$ and the special supercharges $S^\alpha_i$, $\bar S^{\dot\alpha i}$ (the names of [SW, (8)]) it is the quantum-corrected supersymmetry; along the special conformal generators it is the primary condition. The program therefore has two outputs: the quantised interaction, with its counterterms and its quantum master equation, and, for every local operator, its observable and its transformations along all of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$.

Operators. Inserting a composite operator produces divergences, and the limit defining $O[\infty]$ exists for many choices of the functional $O(\varepsilon)$. At scale $\infty$, however, $K_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}K_t=0$ on $\mathbb R^4$, and $P(0,\infty)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ [C07, §1.2] is a contracting homotopy for $Q$: for compactly supported $\alpha$,

where $P(0,\infty)\star$ is the operator with kernel $P(0,\infty)$ [C07, §6.3]. On moment-free Schwartz sections, whose Fourier transforms vanish to infinite order at $p=0$, every $Q$-closed continuous polynomial functional without constant term is $Q$-exact (Chapter 3); on compactly supported sections $Q$ has in addition nonzero classes, among them the pairings with polynomial zero modes of $Q$, finitely many in each polynomial degree and infinitely many in all. An arbitrary $O(\varepsilon)$ therefore gives the zero class on moment-free sections. The content of an operator is the locality of $O(\varepsilon)$: $O(\varepsilon)=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ with local coefficients in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$. Locality and the existence of the limit fix the singular part uniquely, and the finite part is the scheme. An equation expressing $[(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]](x_1)$ as the scale-$\infty$ observable of a second functional has content because that functional is required to be local, and for an operator whose observable is a cocycle, $Q\,O[\infty]=0$ (Chapter 5), anomalous dimensions are read off in the cohomology of local functionals.

Counterterms. The singular part $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is unique (Chapter 4). The cutoff on every edge breaks gauge invariance and superconformal symmetry, and $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ contains $\varepsilon^{-1}$ mass terms with nonzero image under $Q$. The quantum master equation, transported to the UV boundary, then forces finite local counterterms. They are constrained by the master equation and fixed up to a choice; this choice is the renormalisation condition, part of the definition of the quantum theory and of every operator.
The UV boundary. The lower end $t=\varepsilon$ of the Schwinger integral carries two kernels,

the second being [C07, Lemma 10.2.1] with $K_\infty=0$. Edges pinned at $t=\varepsilon$ and carrying $L_\varepsilon$ produce the singular coefficients and the scaling behaviour. Chapter 1 fixes the fields, the odd pairing, the reduced action with its linear differential and vertices, and the classical master equation. Chapter 2 realises $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$ and constructs the equivariant action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$ in the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex. Chapter 3 constructs the Feynman-gauge $Q^{GF}$, records which axioms of [C07, Def 4.3.3] it satisfies, and proves the UV-boundary identity, the acyclicity at scale $\infty$ and the one-loop formula. Chapter 4 computes the one-loop counterterms of the action in the two-, three- and four-point sectors and the quantum master equation at the UV boundary. Chapter 5 computes $O(\varepsilon)$ for the single letters and the scalar bilinears, Chapter 6 their dilatation through the scaling covariance of the regulator, and Chapter 7 the selection rules for the other superconformal components and the program of Steps 2–5.

Translations, rotations and the R-symmetry commute with $Q^{GF}$ and $H$; for gauge-invariant operators their components can be chosen with no one-loop correction, a choice to be realised in Step 2, and the counterterms of the traceless and the trace scalar bilinears stay in their own representations. Along the supercharges, the special supercharges and the special conformal generators the regulator moves, and the one-loop output lies in an explicit list of local structures; under the hypotheses of Proposition [7.13](#b-01296), a local representative and equivariant counterterms, the supercharge component of the traceless scalar bilinear is a multiple of its classical structure.

Every number computed in the following chapters is a coefficient in front of a local functional, and its sign and normalisation are inherited from three classical data: the odd pairing on the fields, the BV action and the linear differential $Q$ [C07, §4.3]. The sources supply the ten-dimensional action [ESW, (31)] and its dimensional reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], while the pairing on the antifields stays implicit in the phrase “natural $(-1)$-shifted symplectic structure” [ESW, Def 1.34]. This chapter fixes all three data for the reduction to Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, writes the interaction vertex by vertex, and shows that the classical master equation determines the relative signs of the pairing.

The ten-dimensional space is $V_{10}=V_{\mathbb R}\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$, where $V_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^{10}$ carries its Euclidean form and the orthogonal decomposition $V_{\mathbb R}=W_{\mathbb R}\oplus W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ of [ESW, §2.2, §2.6]: $W_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^4$ is spacetime and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ consists of the six transverse directions. With $V=W_{\mathbb R}\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$,

and from here on $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ and $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ denote these complexifications. The nondegenerate symmetric form $(-,-)$ of $V_{10}$ is the complex-bilinear extension of the Euclidean form. The letter $W$ alone denotes the multiplicity space of [ESW, §10].

The gauge Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is complex, with bracket $[-,-]$ and a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing $(-,-)$ [ESW, §3.1], chosen positive definite on the compact real form, so that $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ is negative definite on the real slice of [C07, §6.6] (Remark [1.10](#b-00130)). The coupling constant sits in $(-,-)$. The inverse pairing is the element $(-,-)^{-1}\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$.

The map $q\colon\wedge^\bullet V_{10}\to\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$ is antisymmetrisation, $q(v_1\wedge v_2)=v_1v_2-(v_1,v_2)$ [ESW, (29)]. Applied to a two-form, such as $F_A$, the symbol $\rho$ means $\rho\circ q$, as in $\rho(F_A)$ [ESW, (33)].

The exterior derivative $d$ acts along $\mathbb R^4$, and every field is constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The operator $d^*$ is the formal adjoint of $d$ for the Euclidean metric, $\mathrm{dvol}$ is the Euclidean volume density of $\mathbb R^4$, and ${\not d}=\rho\circ d$ is the Dirac operator from $\Sigma$-valued to $\Sigma^*$-valued functions [ESW, §2.1]; the same formula on $\Sigma^*$-valued functions is written ${\not d}|_{\Sigma^*}$.

Fix an orientation of $V$. For an oriented orthonormal basis $v_1,\dots,v_4$ of $V$ the element $q(v_1\wedge v_2\wedge v_3\wedge v_4)=v_1v_2v_3v_4$ of $\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$ depends on the orientation alone. The operator $\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)$ squares to $1$ on $\Sigma$ and on $\Sigma^*$, with eigenvalues $+1$ and $-1$ each of multiplicity $8$. Writing

The element $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ is the antisymmetrisation $q$ of the oriented unit element of $\wedge^4V$, hence depends on the orientation alone. By the Clifford relation the $v_i$ anticommute pairwise and square to $1$, hence

Moving $v_1$ through $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ meets $v_2,v_3,v_4$ once each, so $v_1\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1$; the same holds for each $v_i$, hence for every $v\in V$ by linearity. For $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, $w$ anticommutes with all four $v_i$, so $w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=(+1)(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,w$. Since $\rho(v)$ maps $\Sigma\to\Sigma^*$, the first relation reads $\rho(v)\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)|_{\Sigma}=-\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)|_{\Sigma^*}\rho(v)$, so $\rho(v)$ maps the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $-1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$; the second relation gives $\rho(w)$ mapping the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$. For the multiplicities, take a unit vector $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The even element $v_1w$ satisfies $(v_1w)^2=-v_1^2w^2=-1$ and $v_1w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1w$, so $\rho(v_1w)$ is an invertible endomorphism of $\Sigma$ (and of $\Sigma^*$) exchanging the two eigenspaces of $\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)$; hence each eigenspace has dimension $16/2=8$. ∎

The names of the eigenspaces depend on the orientation of $V$; the opposite orientation exchanges $S_+\leftrightarrow S_-$ in all four of them. This orientation is fixed once; Chapter 2 uses it to name the supercharges.
